text: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string, and deserialize that string back to the original tree. You pick the format. There's no restriction on how it works, as long as the round trip gives back the same tree.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I write two functions, serialize and deserialize. The only rule is that deserialize of serialize of root gives the same shape with the same values. The string is my own format, so nobody else has to read it. And the empty tree is a valid input too. Is that right?
Yes. Your format, your rules. The tree can be empty.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Zero to ten to the fourth nodes, and each value is between minus one thousand and one thousand.

OK. Two things jump out. Values can be negative and up to four digits, like minus one thousand, so my format needs a separator between values. And the tree isn't promised to be balanced; it can be a chain ten thousand deep, so recursion needs care. The key fact: the values alone are not enough. Take one, two and one, null, two. In both, the level-order values are just one, two — but in one, two is a left child, and in the other it's a right child. So I must also write down where the holes are, with a marker n for every null child. Quick check on example one: one, two, three, null, null, four, five. Level by level, I get eleven tokens — five values and six markers — and reading them back gives the same tree. The empty tree should give back empty.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would write only the values and rebuild a tree from them. That's fast, but just wrong: it throws away the shape, and one, two and one, null, two both become one, two. So the real work isn't speed — it's making the format unambiguous. This problem reminds me of level-order traversal with a queue: the bracket format used to display test-case trees is exactly BFS with null holes. The other option is a preorder DFS with null markers. Both work. I'll pick BFS, because it's a plain loop with a queue, so there's no recursion depth to worry about on a ten-thousand-node chain.

Here's the plan. One: serialize with BFS, writing every popped slot — a value and a space, or n for a null. Two: deserialize in the same order: the first token is the root, then each popped node eats two tokens, left then right, and only real children join the queue. Three: on both sides, the empty string means the empty tree. One thing worth flagging — the right child's read isn't checked, and that's safe. n nodes have two n child pointers. Every node except the root fills one of them, so n minus one are real and n plus one are null. That's two n plus one tokens: after the root, exactly two per node. The trade-off: about half the tokens are markers, but trimming trailing ones breaks that count, so I keep them. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Serialize pushes null children too, so it writes a marker for every hole. Deserialize only pushes real nodes, because a null slot has no children to fill, and the while loop's read stops cleanly when the tokens run out. One thing worth flagging — the empty tree. Serialize returns the empty string, and deserialize checks for empty first. The two must match: if I'd encoded the empty tree as n, deserialize would call stoi on n and throw invalid argument. Also, Codec has no member state, so separate Codec objects for the two calls work the same as one shared object.

Let's dry-run the code on example one. In serialize, the row that matters is popping three: node two's two nulls already sit in the queue ahead of three's children, so they're written as n, n before four and five. That's how the string records that two is a leaf. Deserialize then runs exactly five passes for five nodes, two tokens each — one plus ten is eleven, all used. Same tree back. Correct. Corner cases: the empty tree goes to the empty string and back to null. Minus one thousand: stoi reads the whole token, sign and all. One, two and one, null, two give different strings, so no collision. And the trim slip in the table: cutting trailing markers turns one, two into one, two, two, because the failed second read keeps the old word. That's why the count matters.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear both ways: two n plus one slots, each pushed and popped once. Space is linear too. The string is the big part — at most eighty thousand and two characters at ten to the fourth nodes, when every value is minus one thousand. The queue is linear at worst: it peaks at ten thousand and one on a balanced tree, but stays tiny on a chain. In the worst case the tree is a long chain, and that's where BFS pays off: no recursion, so a million-node chain round-trips fine, while a recursive preorder, also correct, crashes on it. Oh, one more thing — bad input. A cut-off string won't crash, it quietly builds a wrong tree: one, two gives one with two children of two. For a real service, I'd check the second read and reject bad strings.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed why the format must be unambiguous: null markers so one, two and one, null, two don't collide, and a separator for values like minus one thousand. You proved the two n plus one token count, used it to explain why the unchecked second read is safe, and showed how trimming trailing markers breaks it. And you picked BFS for a reason: no recursion, so a million-node chain works where recursive preorder crashes, with the empty tree kept as the empty string on both sides. Good work.
